alalal-e90422-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 10: whether Lombard sufficiently gives the kinds of credibles.

alalal-e90422-d1e117.summary: Introduces the question on Augustine's statement in Lombard's text that some things we do not believe unless we understand them.

alalal-e90422-d1e131.summary: Introduces objections that Lombard lists the credibles incompletely.

alalal-e90422-d1e139.summary: First objection: Augustine's original, in the Eighty-three Questions, adds a further kind, things always believed and never understood, such as the history of all past events, which Lombard omits.

alalal-e90422-d1e155.summary: Second objection: Lombard implies, and the original says, that in divine matters one must first believe and then understand, but this does not hold of everything divine, such as that God is one.

alalal-e90422-d1e168.summary: Third objection: there is no assent unless one first understands at least what the words mean, so understanding precedes every belief, which the text denies.

alalal-e90422-d1e181.summary: Fourth objection: the Gloss on 2 Corinthians 3:5 says nothing is believed unless first thought.

alalal-e90422-d1e192.summary: Solution: regarding assent to what precedes and follows the articles, there are three kinds of credibles: what is always believed and never understood, the history of the canonical books; believing that precedes understanding, for credibles reason can reach; and believing that precedes understanding of truth for credibles reason does not grasp, like the Trinity. Lombard intends only the last two, so he omits the first.
claims: There are three kinds of credibles: canonical history, truths reason can reach, and truths beyond reason.

alalal-e90422-d1e229.summary: This answers the first and second objections.

alalal-e90422-d1e237.summary: Reply to the third: Albert grants that understanding what the words mean precedes every belief, but Lombard speaks of understanding the reality, not the words.
claims: Grasping the meaning of words precedes all belief, while understanding of the reality may follow it.
concepts: intellectus quid nominis vs intellectus rei

alalal-e90422-d1e253.summary: Reply to the fourth: the Gloss speaks of faith as coming from hearing, or of understanding what the words mean.

alalal-e90422.summary: Article 10 asks whether Lombard's account of the kinds of credibles, following Augustine, is complete, since Augustine also names things always believed and never understood, such as history. Albert distinguishes three kinds of credibles: canonical history, always believed and never understood; truths that reason can reach, where belief precedes understanding; and truths beyond reason, such as the Trinity, where belief precedes understanding of the truth. Lombard addresses only the last two. Grasping what the words mean precedes all belief, but Lombard speaks of understanding the reality itself.
claims: Credibles are of three kinds: canonical history, truths accessible to reason, and truths beyond reason.
Understanding the meaning of words precedes belief, while understanding of the reality may follow it.
